(a) Repeal.—
        (1) In general.—Section 1513 of the Strom Thurmond National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1999 (Public Law 105–261; 112 Stat. 2174; 22 U.S.C. 2778 note) is amended by striking subsection (a). 
        (2) Conforming amendment.—Subsection (c) of such section is amended by striking “(1) Subsection (a)” and all that follows through “(2) The amendments” and inserting “The amendments”.  
    (b) Additional Determination and Report.—Accompanying but separate from the submission to Congress of the first notification after the date of the enactment of this Act under section 38(f) of the Arms Export Control Act (22 U.S.C. 2778(f)) relating to the removal of satellites and related items from the United States Munitions List, the President shall also submit to Congress—
        (1) a determination by the President that the removal of such satellites and items from the United States Munitions List is in the national security interests of the United States; and 
        (2) a report identifying and analyzing any differences between—
            (A) the recommendations and draft regulations for controlling the export, re-export, and transfer of such satellites and related items that were submitted in the report to Congress required by section 1248 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2010 (Public Law 111–84; 123 Stat. 2546); and 
            (B) the final regulations under which the export, re-export, and transfer of such satellites and related items would continue to be controlled.   
    (c) Prohibition.—
        (1) In general.—Subject to paragraph (3), no satellites or related items that are made subject to the Export Administration Regulations (15 CFR part 730 et seq.) as a result of the enactment of subsection (a) of this section, whether or not enumerated on the Commerce Control List—
            (A) may be exported, re-exported, or transferred, directly or indirectly, to—
                (i) any government of a country described in paragraph (2); or 
                (ii) any entity or person in or acting for or on behalf of such government, entity, or person; or  
            (B) may be launched in a country described in paragraph (2) or as part of a launch vehicle owned, operated, or manufactured by the government of such country or any entity or person in or acting for or on behalf of such government, entity, or person.  
        (2) Countries described.—The countries referred to in paragraph (1) are the following:
            (A) The People’s Republic of China. 
            (B) North Korea. 
            (C) Any country that is a state sponsor of terrorism.  
        (3) Waiver.—The President may waive the prohibition in paragraph (1) on a case-by-case basis if not later than 30 days before doing so the President—
            (A) determines that it is in the national interest of the United States to do so; and 
            (B) notifies the appropriate congressional committees of such determination.   
    (d) Presumption of Denial.—Any license or other authorization to export satellites and related items to a country with respect to which the United States maintains a comprehensive arms embargo shall be subject to a presumption of denial. 
    (e) Report.—
        (1) In general.—Not later than one year after the date of the enactment of this Act, and annually thereafter, the Director of National Intelligence, in consultation with the Secretary of State, shall submit to the appropriate congressional committees a report on efforts of state sponsors of terrorism, other foreign countries, or entities to illicitly acquire satellites and related items. 
        (2) Form.—The report required by paragraph (1) shall be submitted in unclassified form, but may contain a classified annex.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the consultation, the notifications, and the mention of "final regulations" amount to participation. But every actor is inside the federal government: the President reports to and notifies Congress, and the Director of National Intelligence consults the Secretary of State. The reference to final regulations only describes the content of a report to Congress; it does not grant or require rulemaking, a comment period, or any outside-party role.
fable.s: the Director of National Intelligence, in consultation with the Secretary of State, shall submit to the appropriate congressional committees a report

qwen_block.w: The section requires the President to submit reports and determinations to Congress. Congress is part of the federal government, so this interaction is internal to the government and does not constitute participation by outside parties. The other provisions involve prohibitions on exports, waivers by the President (with notification to Congress), and reports by federal intelligence officials to Congress, none of which involve consultation with or input from non-federal entities like the public, states, or private companies in the decision-making process.

opus.w: Every procedure here stays inside the federal government: the DNI consults the Secretary of State, and the President and DNI report to or notify Congress and its committees. The mention of 'draft regulations' and 'final regulations' only asks for a report comparing existing rules; it does not require or authorize rulemaking. The presumption of denial is about export license applications, which do not count as participation. No state, company, expert, or member of the public is consulted, and no one outside the government is given a right to sue or object.
opus.s: the Director of National Intelligence, in consultation with the Secretary of State, shall submit to the appropriate congressional committees a report
opus.b:
**Label: No.** I checked who is involved in each procedure. Every actor is inside the federal government, or the provision is a licensing rule.

**Tempting misreadings, and why they fail:**
- **Reports and notices to Congress.** Subsection (b) and the waiver in (c)(3) require reports, determinations and notices to Congress and its committees. Congress is inside the federal government, so these don't count.
- **"Consultation."** In (e), the Director of National Intelligence consults with the Secretary of State. That is coordination between two federal officials, not with outsiders.
- **"Draft regulations" and "final regulations."** Subsection (b)(2) only asks for a report comparing regulations that already exist. It does not require or authorize any new rulemaking or comment period.
- **Presumption of denial.** Subsection (d) concerns export license applications, and applying for a license is not participation.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires reports to Congress and consultation between federal officials (Director of National Intelligence and Secretary of State). Congress and federal agencies are inside the federal government. There is no requirement to consult with states, tribes, the public, or other outside entities before making a decision.
qwen_chat.s:
(e) Report.—
        (1) In general.—Not later than one year after the date of the enactment of this Act, and annually thereafter, the Director of National Intelligence, in consultation with the Secretary of State, shall submit to the appropriate congressional committees a report on efforts of state sponsors of terrorism, other foreign countries, or entities to illicitly acquire satellites and related items.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the requirement for the Director of National Intelligence to act "in consultation with the Secretary of State" constitutes participation. However, both the Director of National Intelligence and the Secretary of State are federal officials inside the executive branch. Intra-governmental coordination does not count as participation under the definition, which requires interaction with parties *outside* the federal government (such as states, tribes, the public, or private entities). The other interactions described are reports to Congress (also inside the government) or prohibitions on exports, which do not involve outside parties in the decision-making process.
